reviewer: Claude agent review (Opus), not a human historian
text: 2026-10-23: the book was rewritten to the storytelling template (README §6) and approved on an independent review: every scene paragraph, imageAlt and dramatised note was checked against facts.json and research/rashtrakuta-verified.md, the 12 pictures were opened, and Ganitasarasangraha 1.3–6 was checked in Rangacharya's 1912 translation. The prose names five people and gives four dates; the climax (the walk to the goddess and the bound hand) is scene 11 and scene 12 the resolution.

The finger scene is faithful to Sanjan v.47 (left finger, Mahalakshmi, a calamity to the whole people), with nothing shown or exaggerated, and the cut-or-symbolic, Kolhapur and epidemic readings are disclosed on the last page.

Fixed on review: the great-great-grandson wording in scene-05's note, which had slipped back; a false 'did not praise him for war' about the mathematician (vv.5–6 do); the six-seasons line contradicting the plague; the messenger's direction and unsourced feudatories in the son's revolt; and an undisclosed reason for the king's return after abdicating. The king's choice in the revolt is now shown and disclosed as invented.

Scene 9 rests on the Konnur record, a 12th-century copy that Kielhorn called spurious and Bhandarkar partly vindicated, and is disclosed as such; the rebel son's identity and fate, and whether he was the successor, are left unstated, as in the records.

Newcomer test (README §7): (1) yes, a first-time reader can say who he was, what he wanted (to be 'the lord who protects the humble'), what happened and why it matters; (2) yes, the prophecy and the drums' promise pay off, the walk without crown or army is the turning point and the charter's Sibi and Dadhichi line is the goosebump moment; scenes 5 to 8 are the flattest stretch. Owner note: the scene-12 picture's left hand reads as whole at book size.

2026-10-11: approved on a second full read of story.json (introduction, twelve scenes with titles, alt texts, paragraphs, facts and dramatised lists, summary, ನಿಮಗೆ ಗೊತ್ತೇ?, visitToday, provenance, disclosure, content note) after the first pass returned five text blockers and two image blockers, all now fixed.

Blockers found on the first pass and fixed before approval: (1) 'the first Kannada book' in the teaser, introduction, scene-10, scene-12 and the collections.json description, though the Kavirajamarga itself names earlier Kannada poets; now 'the oldest surviving Kannada book' everywhere, with the earlier poets noted in scene-10's dramatised list. (2) A wrong generation count: Krishna III and Govinda IV are Amoghavarsha's great-great-grandsons (A-I, Krishna II, Jagattunga, Indra III or Amoghavarsha III, then Govinda IV or Krishna III); scene-05 and the f-vingavalli fact are corrected. (3) The ring inscription was credited to the continuator of Sulaiman's book; it is Ibn Khurdadba's, an independent geographer, and scene-08 now says so. (4) Scene-09 said the Ganitasarasangraha had no praise of god and 'a thousand problems'; it opens with a salutation to Mahavira Jina, and the count is now 'hundreds'. (5) Scene-07 stated as fact that the rebel son survived and was never named on stone; both sentences are gone and the dramatised note now says the record does not tell who the son was or what became of him.

Nits fixed on the same pass: ಅರವತ್ತು spelling; Sulaiman 'included him' rather than 'wrote his name'; scene-11 now 'for years' the six seasons were safe (no contradiction with the epidemic), ಮಾರಿ for the loanword ಪ್ಲೇಗು, Altekar's reading given as an epidemic, the unverified Settar and Desai names replaced by 'some historians'; Indra IV called the last heir of the Rattas, with the Bankapura coronation site disclosed as the historians' identification; the 866 eclipse placed in the afternoon (Fleet: 9 h 4 min after sunrise) without claiming totality at Nilgund; the Sanjan find no longer 'in the soil'; ಸೋದರ for the Gupta king's brother; Manyakheta 'copper plates go out from here' instead of 'every copper plate'; Sulaiman sailed from the Persian Gulf (Siraf dropped, being only background research); the scene-01 note now separates the rainy-season camp at Sribhavana (two grants) from the birth there (editors' inference); the 1150-year estimate disclosed in scene-10.

The storytelling rule checked: scene prose has no 'historians think', 'disputed', 'perhaps' and no scholar name; caveats, scholars and tiers sit in dramatised lists and facts. Every deliberate choice is disclosed in its own scene: birth at Sribhavana near the Narmada c. 800 (scene-01); fourteen at accession as an estimate, eleven to fifteen (scene-02); Patalamalla as an old household commander and teacher, Karka and Patalamalla as two men (scene-04); Vingavalli in the Vengi country, and the battle in his youth (scene-05); Manyakheta built in his youth (scene-06); the son unnamed, the Konnur record's 12th-century copy and Kielhorn's doubt (scene-07); Sulaiman at a Konkan port and never meeting the king, Balhara as a historians' identification (scene-08); one visit to Jinasena, Mahaviracharya at the same court, Gunabhadra writing after the reign (scene-09); the poet as Srivijaya, Pathak against Fleet (scene-10); the calamity as an epidemic, the Kolhapur goddess as the editors' inference, the finger actually cut as the 1925 reading with the symbolic reading named, sixteen years before 871 as a story choice (scene-11); abdications as retreats to the Jain teachers, Prasnottara attribution disputed, death at Manyakheta c. 878 as convention, sallekhana left out as speculation (scene-12).

Every name, number, year, relationship and quotation was compared with facts.json and research/rashtrakuta-verified.md: Sanjan vv. 23–28 (Himalaya springs, Dharma and Chakrayudha, Maharaja Sarva pun, the astrologers' Himalaya-to-Setu and the fetters released only in ashes), v. 35 (Govinda's last words), vv. 36–37 (lion-throne, the dhakka proclamation), vv. 38–41 (sixteen principalities, false oaths, officers killed, beasts, the setting sun and the crooked ones, Arya Patalamalla as the rising mountain, elders and the wise), vv. 43–46 (medicine and fuel, pearls and elephants, lords waiting at the gate), v. 47 (Jimutaketu's son, Sibi, Dadhichi, Vira-Narayana's left finger to Mahalakshmi), v. 48 (the Gupta donor, 'of what account are external objects', more than once), v. 49 (six seasons), the grant (Uttarayana in Pausha, Saka 793, Manyakheta, four Brahmans, a village near Sanjan), the seal (Garuda on a lotus, a snake in each hand, Srimad-Amoghavarshadevasya), the Parsi friend; Dhruva II's Baroda plates of 835 (unsheathed sword, tributary rebels after promised obedience, Amoghavarsha speedily placed on his throne); Cambay v. 12 (Yama's morsels at Vingavalli) and Karhad vv. 13–14 (Manyakheta deriding Indra's city, the fire that burnt the Chalukya race); Konnur (Kedala, Talakad, the Kaveri, recall for the son's revolt, the lunar eclipse of 860, Bankesa's sanctuary at Kolanura, Bankapura); Sulaiman 851 in Elliot and Dowson (four kings, ears pierced, pay as among the Arabs, horses and elephants, fifty-year reigns, partial to the Arabs), Abu Zaid's 'king of kings' and Ibn Khurdadba's ring; Gunabhadra's foot-dust and 'today I am purified'; Jinasena's paramaguru title and closing wish; Jayadhavala Saka 759 (837); Mahaviracharya ch. 1 vv. 3–8; Kavirajamarga 1.36–38, the Nripatungadevanumata colophons and 3.217; the Prasnottararatnamalika colophon and its Tibetan version; Nilgund and Sirur of 16 June 866 in the fifty-second year with Vanga, Anga, Magadha, Malava, Vengi and the umbrellas, chowries, pali-dhvaja, conches, tivili and Garuda crest; the Kanheri date Saka 799 (877–78) and Fleet's sixty-two full years.

Kannada: adult told-story register, no vulgarity; no em dash anywhere; NFC. The content note (war, officers murdered, epidemic, the finger, a Digambara monk) is truthful. The summary states only what the scenes tell. story.facts is byte-identical to facts.json (39 facts); every scene facts[] id and didYouKnow id resolves and every fact is used; each scene's facts[] covers its recorded claims; the disputed notes in facts.json carry both readings for every contested point.

Rashtrakuta dynasty entry in collections.json checked against research/rashtrakuta.md §1 and Appendix B: years 753–982, capital (Ellora region and Mayurakhandi, then Manyakheta), Dantidurga's Hiranyagarbha with the Gurjara door-keepers (Sanjan v. 9), Krishna I and Ellora as a historians' identification, Dhruva and the Gauda umbrellas (v. 14), Govinda III to the Himalaya and Kanchi, Krishna II and Kokkala's daughter (Cambay v. 14), Indra III and Mahodaya, Govinda IV weighed against gold, Krishna III at Takkola, Indra IV grandson of Krishna III dying in 982; the dating paragraph names only the inscriptional anchors as fixed and now says the list is a selection. The description now says 'the oldest surviving Kannada book'.

2026-10-11, after approval: three wording nits applied by the author (stale clause removed from scene-03 dramatised; introduction no longer claims a first naming; summary says ಉಳಿದ ಗ್ರಂಥ); storySha256 recomputed; no fact or picture changed.
illustrations: All thirteen WebPs (cover, scene-01 to scene-12, 1600x900) were opened and compared with their scene paragraphs, alt texts and bible/style.md, with enlarged crops of the banners, seals, swords, riders' feet, hands, books and the copper plates. Three pictures were regenerated after the first pass and re-checked; this approval hashes the replaced files.

Image blockers on the first pass, fixed: scene-05 showed a gold Roman-aquila eagle standard and heraldic eagle banners; it now shows the seal Garuda (human-bodied, beaked, winged, squatting on a lotus, a snake in each hand) on a cloth banner and on the howdah shield. scene-10 showed the poet reading from a bound codex; it now shows a tied palm-leaf pothi. scene-11 was also redone: the whole left hand is now bound in white, and the marigolds (a post-16th-century introduction) are gone, replaced by hibiscus and jasmine.

Lead consistency: the same man in every picture that shows him, a long oval face, fine high-bridged nose, thin moustache, no beard, long loose black hair and a low gold band: the boy on the lion-throne in scene-02; the young man on horseback in scene-04, on the war elephant in scene-05, among the builders in scene-06, before the basadi in scene-07; the king kneeling at the guru's feet in scene-09, on the throne in scene-10 and on the cover; the grey-haired elder in scene-11 and scene-12. He is handsome and strong throughout. bible/style.md was updated to clean-shaven with no scar to match.

cover: the king on a palace terrace above the river at sunset, three white umbrellas, chowries, straight sword, a tied leaf manuscript, war elephants and new building below. Nit: the banner Garuda is drawn as a heraldic bird holding snakes, not the seated seal Garuda.

scene-01: monsoon night camp, Govinda III with the newborn in a lamplit tent, astrologers, elephants under shelters, a flooded river. Nit: one astrologer holds an armillary sphere (plausible as an Indian gola-yantra).
scene-02: the boy king on a black stone lion-throne under three umbrellas with chowries, chiefs bowing, drummers at the gate. Clean.
scene-03: burning officer's house, riders with loot, a torn Garuda banner (bird form holding snakes) in the mud. Nit: two-storey balconied houses look late.

scene-04: dawn on a red-earth plain, the young king between grey-bearded Patalamalla in studded leather and Karka with a drawn straight sword, elephants and banners behind. Nits: the banner Garuda is a heraldic bird; Patalamalla's sandal sits in a strap loop at the frame edge (toe-loop stirrups are attested in India much earlier); Karka has a moustache where the bible says clean-shaven.

scene-05 (regenerated): the young king drawing a bow on an elephant, the seal Garuda banner, elephants colliding, round shields, a river behind. Nit: an enemy saddle-cloth carries a stylised leaf emblem.
scene-06: the king pointing among masons, brick-carrying elephants, timber cranes and scaffolds on a river bend. Clean.

scene-07: lunar eclipse over a stone basadi, the plumed general kneeling with a cloth-wrapped petition, the king, the monk seated in the porch in side view with a pichchi, torches. Clean; alt text corrected to match.

scene-08: Konkan harbour, two-masted lateen-rigged plank ships, pepper sacks, Sulaiman bearded in a plain wrapped turban writing on a tablet, local officials with heavy gold ear-rings, elephants. Nit: a generic hill fort far behind.
scene-09: the king kneeling at the feet of the old monk on a stone bench in side view, no frontal nudity, a seated Jina in the sanctum, scholars with leaf bundles. Clean.

scene-10 (regenerated): the poet with a hair knot reading from a palm-leaf pothi before the king on the lion-throne under three umbrellas, a painted cloth of rivers behind. Nit: the poet has a thin moustache where the bible says clean-shaven.

scene-11 (regenerated): the grey-haired king in white stepping out of a small dark stone shrine, the whole left hand bound in white with no blood, the priest turned away, hibiscus, jasmine and lamps. Clean.

scene-12: the elder at a stone window above the river at dawn, three copper plates on a ring with a seal on the sill, his left hand out of sight. Nit: the seal shows a bird-form Garuda without the lotus or snakes.

No image shows a helmet, mail, Mughal or Ottoman dress, a tall kirita or full beard on the king, the present Kolhapur temple or Malkhed fort, gunpowder, European ships, modern letters, gore, the finger being cut, or close frontal nudity of a monk; no extra hands or fingers were found.
limitations: This is an AI review by a Claude agent; no human historian or epigraphist has read the text or checked the images.

Fact checking was limited to research/rashtrakuta.md and research/rashtrakuta-verified.md and did not re-fetch the primary editions; the Ganitasarasangraha opening salutation was checked from the reviewer's knowledge of Rangacharya's 1912 translation because archive.org returned errors during the review.

Not read at first hand by anyone on this project: Settar and Desai on the finger as a symbolic offering, Altekar's 'epidemic' (known only through Chronology of Gujarat p. 360), the Kanheri inscription text, the Surat plates of Karka, the Deoli plates' wording, Pathak's 1898 Kavirajamarga, the Uttarapurana colophon date (Saka 820 or 824), the name of the Eastern Chalukya king at Vingavalli, and the son named in Konnur v. 31.

The Bankapura site of Indra IV's coronation and Bankapura's naming after Bankesa are historians' identifications; the identification of Balhara with the Rashtrakuta Vallabha and of the Kavirajamarga's four towns are modern scholarship.

No portrait, sculpture or coin with Amoghavarsha's face survives; his face, every other face, the camp, the courts, Manyakheta, the Kolhapur shrine and the Konkan harbour are invented, as the disclosure says.

Remaining small image nits were recorded and not regenerated: heraldic-bird Garudas on the cover and scene-04 banners and the scene-12 seal; a strap loop under Patalamalla's sandal in scene-04; moustaches on Karka (scene-04) and Srivijaya (scene-10); late-looking houses in scene-03.
